Question: Is there something in between free open-source games and Kickstarter projects?

Just in case...

This is something someone told me not long ago: have no shame in using the tools you have available; only those who have taken the step to create something new know the hardships that come with entrepreneurship.

To put it in perspective, not many (if any) entrepreneur refrained from using the wealth of their family or connections to start their own projects. Since not all of us have wealthy families or connections, the traditional tools to start our projects are greatly reduced.

This is when Crowdfunding enters the equation. Yes, gaming projects have a spotty reputation but there are also great success stories. Remember, at the end of the day it's just a tool and as such, its potential depends entirely in how you use it.

If you do your homework, know your limitations, work diligently and with integrity, then you have all it takes to have a proper crowndfunding campaign. Yes shit happens, good communication and honesty can do wonders.

Of course, you probably have your reasons to avoid this option, if that's the case the other options are living out of your family while you develop, work a good paying job and save for years to start your project or compromise your development time with a regular work. As you may imagine this solutions are not for everyone or for every product... but welp.

Yes, there is one example I can think of and that is Warzone 2100.

Warzone 2100 was originally developed as a commercial game by Pumpkin Studios and published in 1999, and was released as open source by them in 2004, for the community to continue working on it.

Interestingly the game received its latest update fairly recently. I guess this is one of the benefits of open source games; the fans can continue to develop the game, when there is no financial gain to be had for the original developer.

2016-07-10 After 3.5 years of development, version 3.2.0 of Warzone has finally been released.

If you want to look for more examples, a good place to check is this list of open source games.

I would say the middle ground between completely free games (never ask for money) and ones that want money before they develop them would be games that get developed and then ask for money though that is pretty much the standard system.

The issue with your idea is that if it will be free people will wait instead of spending money up front, it would be better to just make it cheap. But that only works when trying to get a company name out, and that seems a dead system to me anyhow as developers come and go while publishers just leach off them then move on never taking a huge risk themselves. The biggest issue for free is no marketing budget to get news of it out.

While I have brought up the kickstarter model many times to other devs/contributors of the Terasology project (like the way krita is FLOSS but also does kickstarter goals), we have decided we won't be doing that any time soon, and a working on a better base before we attempt that. However you can donate money to the project and put bounties on certain features/bugs. So there is that.
